description: Team from Azerbaijan at NASA Space Apps Vilnius. We’re building Solar Guardian: health software that helps astronauts act on their own health on long missions. It links live NASA space weather data (solar storms, radiation) with a personal digital twin of each astronaut and 2-minute cognitive mini-games that catch fatigue early. We bring Linux (Red Hat certified) and AI app development (Python, Flask, cloud).
summary: Solar Guardian is a crew-facing self-care app for long-duration missions. On the way to Mars a message to Earth takes 3–22 minutes one way, so astronauts must manage most health issues on board. Solar Guardian compares wearable vitals, sleep, exercise logs, cabin CO₂, radiation dose and the crew schedule with each astronaut's personal 14-day baseline. When the data changes and the schedule cannot explain it, the app asks one short question (for example, why the heart rate went up), applies simple transparent rules, and tells the astronaut what to do: nothing, self-care, follow-up, or contact the Crew Medical Officer. If several crew members change at the same time, it checks the cabin air first. An emergency mode guides the crew step by step through chest pain, an unresponsive crewmate and CPR in weightlessness, while showing the real Earth–Mars signal delay from NASA's Deep Space Network. Everything goes into a structured report for the CMO. The design follows NASA's ExMC clinical decision support and Earth-Independent Medical Operations concepts.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Solar Guardian is a prototype of the crew-facing front end of an onboard clinical decision support system, as described by NASA's Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC). Sensors show what changed; only the astronaut knows why. The app joins these two:

- Today: plain-language status cards (heart, sleep, cabin air, radiation) and one question at a time when something needs context.

- My body: an interactive 3D body with seven systems coloured green/amber/red, a live ECG, vitals and a timeline of heart rate and cabin CO₂ against the crew schedule.

- Log & messages: symptom reporting, a daily food/water/exercise log (as on the ISS), and a private message to the flight surgeon or psychologist that stays out of the crew report.

- Health items & report: open items with follow-up status (improved / no change / worsened / resolved), each classified with the NASA Integrated Medical Model categories; a report for the CMO in text and machine-readable JSON.

- Emergency: guided steps for chest pain, unresponsiveness and CPR (including microgravity CPR methods), with a 3D view comparing the ISS (under 1 s delay) and Mars, using today's real light time from NASA DSN Now.

HOW IT WORKS

Each deviation (short sleep, stopped exercise, unexplained heart-rate rise) is checked against the crew schedule and personal baseline. If it is unexplained, the crew member answers with one tap. Transparent rules, shown next to every result, decide the outcome. Example: two stress-related heart-rate rises in 24 h → CMO check-in. Red-flag symptoms always go to the CMO immediately. A crew-wide pattern with high CO₂ points to the environment instead of the person.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Supports Earth-independent medical care when ground help is minutes away.

- Astronauts are not doctors: plain words, "how to measure" guides, and clear next steps.

- Saves CMO time with structured, context-rich reports ready for decision-support tools such as the NASA–Google CMO-DA concept.

- Protects privacy: private conferences are kept separate from crew data.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file, three.js (WebGL) for the 3D body and Earth–Mars link, Canvas for the ECG, SVG for the charts, BroadcastChannel for the SOS link to the CMO console, and the NASA DSN Now XML feed for live light time. No backend; it runs in any browser.

CREATIVITY

Instead of more alarms, the app asks the astronaut for context and explains every decision. It separates "my body" from "our cabin", and it makes the communication delay visible during an emergency.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Communication delay, crew workload, astronauts without medical training, privacy, accessibility (slow pulse animation, reduced-motion support), and safety: data is simulated, it is not a medical device, and real thresholds would be set by flight surgeons.
